related_questions.snippet: Gender: People assigned female at birth are much more likely to develop breast cancer than others. Age: Breast cancer risk increases with age, with most breast cancers developing after the age of 50. Genetic mutations: Inherited gene mutations cause approximately five to 10 percent of diagnosed breast cancers.

text_blocks.snippet: Breast cancer risk factors can be broadly categorized as lifestyle-related, reproductive factors, genetic factors, and other factors. Lifestyle choices like alcohol consumption, obesity, and lack of physical activity can increase risk, as can reproductive history including early menstruation, late menopause, and not breastfeeding. Family history and genetic mutations (like in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes) also play a significant role. Additionally, factors like age, radiation exposure, and certain breast conditions can elevate risk.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle-related, reproductive factors, genetic factors, and other factors

list.title: Alcohol:
list.snippet: Increased alcohol consumption is linked to a higher risk, with the risk increasing with the amount consumed.

list.title: Weight:
list.snippet: Being overweight or obese, especially after menopause, is associated with increased risk.

list.title: Physical Activity:
list.snippet: A sedentary lifestyle and lack of physical activity can also contribute to higher risk.

list.title: Smoking:
list.snippet: Smoking has been linked to a higher risk, particularly for younger, premenopausal women.
Age at Menarche: Starting menstruation before age 12 increases risk.
Age at Menopause: Starting menopause after age 55 is linked to a higher risk.
Age at First Birth: Women who have their first child after age 35 or who never have children have an increased risk.
Breastfeeding: Not breastfeeding is associated with a slightly increased risk.

list.title: Family History:
list.snippet: Having a family history of breast or ovarian cancer increases the likelihood of developing the disease.

list.title: BRCA1 and BRCA2 Genes:
list.snippet: Mutations in these genes are strongly linked to increased breast cancer risk.

list.title: Radiation Exposure:
list.snippet: Previous radiation therapy to the chest area, especially at a young age, can increase risk.

list.title: Dense Breast Tissue:
list.snippet: Women with dense breasts (more glandular tissue than fatty tissue) have a higher risk.

list.title: Age:
list.snippet: The risk of breast cancer increases with age, with most cases diagnosed in women over 50.

list.title: Certain Benign Breast Conditions:
list.snippet: Conditions like atypical hyperplasia can elevate risk.

list.title: Hormone Replacement Therapy:
list.snippet: Long-term use of combined hormone replacement therapy during menopause is associated with increased risk.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that many of these factors can be modified through lifestyle changes, and early detection through screening is crucial for improving outcomes, says the American Cancer Society.
